source.title: [Paper] A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders

record.file_problem: The complete LessWrong post is supplied; the linked arXiv paper itself is not included.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports experiments on SAE feature reliability and absorption that qualify the idea that SAE latents are interpretable, complete features; it does not test toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The post reports results from a first-letter task and causal interventions. It gives no per-SAE precision, recall, or absorption-rate values in the supplied text. Hyperparameter variation is reported qualitatively; it is recorded as one aggregate result rather than as separate settings.
record.test_reason: The study's own experiments on over 200 Gemma Scope SAEs in Gemma-2-2b show latents that seem to track first-letter features but fail on arbitrary tokens. Absorbing latents mediate the information instead. This bears directly on whether SAE features are complete units (V5) and qualifies how fully SAEs recover sparse features (V4).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that the result concerns measurement error in the SAE method, not how the model represents letters. Linear probes show the first-letter direction is present. They attribute absorption to the sparsity objective acting on co-occurring dense and sparse features, and expect it to generalize beyond spelling.
record.recipe_differences: This is an SAE interpretability study using first-letter classification and causal mediation in Gemma-2-2b, rather than toy networks and geometric measurements of superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: Absorption rate varies with SAE size and sparsity; the post gives no per-setting values or direction of change.
record.problems: The post identifies limitations: one leverage model (Gemma-2-2b), one SAE architecture (JumpReLU), and one task (first-letter identification). The supplied summary gives no numerical outcome values or uncertainty estimates for the reported comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No reported experimental result bearing on the claim was left out. Discussion comments and cited findings from other work were not recorded as study results.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, geometry or sparsity transition.
All: capacity competition and dedicated dimensions are not examined. The comments speculate but report no results.
All: neuron polysemanticity causes are not studied.
Feature spread across neurons; other models, tasks and feature types; other SAE architectures.
Stability across training runs/seeds, canonicity across SAE architectures, and feature types other than first-letter.
All: dimensionality of features is not examined.

missing.what: Quantitative precision/recall per SAE, absorption rates versus width and L0, and the ablation-based absorption metric values. These are in the arXiv paper, which is not supplied.

Author comment (chanind): 'partial absorption' exists, where the main latent fires weakly and both latents have an ablation effect. The paper's metric counts only full non-firing, so it likely understates absorption.
Author comment (Joseph Bloom): no set of 26 SAE latents could be found that causally mediated spelling, unlike probes.

record.verdict_notes: Only the LessWrong summary is available, so all rows are qualitative. The post is author-written about their own paper and is not an original source for the claim. The V4 link is weaker than V5: the study is framed as SAE unreliability, not as evidence about whether sparse features exist in the model.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, overlapping near-orthogonal feature directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition, and whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study tests SAE recovery of first-letter information in Gemma-2-2b, not feature spread across many neurons or recovery across other models, tasks, and feature types.
The study tests completeness/reliability for first-letter information, but does not establish stability across training runs or that SAE features are canonical units in general.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated SAE latents as classifiers of first-letter information and compared their precision and recall with linear probes.
rows.measure: Precision and recall of SAE latents tracking first-letter information
rows.value: The post says SAE latents were unreliable classifiers and performed much worse than linear probes; no numerical precision or recall values are stated.
rows.note: The post says precision and recall were measured but supplies no values in this summary. It reports results over more than 200 SAEs without separate per-SAE outcomes.
rows.check: Subject is better stated as Gemma Scope JumpReLU SAEs on Gemma-2-2b. The linear-probe baseline is appropriate. For V5 the latents are clearly incomplete classifiers, so partial in recovery terms and contrary to V5's completeness. The post gives no precision or recall numbers.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b
rows.operation_detail: Examined SAE-latent activation and causal mediation of first-letter information, including absorbing latents.
rows.measure: Whether SAE latents track and causally mediate first-letter information
rows.baseline: Linear probes are described as having much better recall; no numerical baseline is stated for this causal measure.
rows.value: Some latents appeared to track an interpretable first-letter feature but failed on examples where it should apply; roughly token-aligned absorbing latents weakly projected onto the feature direction and causally mediated in place of the main latent.
rows.note: The post describes causal interventions as part of its absorption metric but does not give numerical intervention effects here.
rows.check: Fine as a row. The main latent fails on some examples and token-aligned absorbing latents carry the feature, so the feature is recovered only incompletely and split across non-canonical latents.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b
rows.operation_detail: Varied SAE size and sparsity and assessed how absorption changed.
rows.value: The post says absorption rate varies with SAE size and sparsity, and that the experiments suggest tuning is unlikely to remove absorption entirely; no values or directions for individual settings are stated.
rows.locator: Feature Absorption is problematic; hyperparameter discussion
rows.note: The post reports the variation and tuning conclusion qualitatively, without separate outcomes for particular sizes or sparsity settings.
rows.check: No per-setting values or direction of change are given. The key stated result is that absorption is likely robust to tuning: completeness failure persists across the size and sparsity settings tested.

relationships.condition: Gemma-2-2b, first-letter task, Gemma Scope JumpReLU SAEs
relationships.reason: SAE latents recover first-letter features only unreliably and far worse than linear probes, though probes show the information is linearly present (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: SAE latents tracked first-letter features unreliably and far worse than linear probes, even though the probes show the information is linearly present.

relationships.condition: Gemma-2-2b, first-letter task, over 200 Gemma Scope JumpReLU SAEs across sizes/sparsities
relationships.reason: Apparent first-letter latents fail on arbitrary tokens, absorbing token-aligned latents causally mediate instead, and absorption persists under hyperparameter tuning (r1, r2, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Latents that looked like first-letter features failed to fire on arbitrary tokens, token-aligned latents that absorbed the feature carried the causal effect instead, and absorption persisted under hyperparameter tuning.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
